methods.title: Methods
methods.intro: Every study on this page follows the same rules. They are deliberately conservative: the aim is to make a false positive hard to produce, even at the cost of rejecting some real but small effects.

items.name: Data
items.text: Free daily data only: yfinance OHLCV for about 23 cross-asset ETFs and the S&P 500, point-in-time S&P 500 membership from 1996 (so backtests only trade names that were in the index on each date), and FRED for macro series. Every result records its data vintage.

items.name: Execution
items.text: Signals are computed at the close; fills happen at the next day's open, with 7 bps of slippage on every trade. No midpoint fills and no same-close trading.

items.name: Validation
items.text: Rules-based strategies have no fitted parameters, so the whole history is out-of-sample. Learned components are trained walk-forward, with purged K-fold or combinatorial purged cross-validation (CPCV), and are never fitted on the test window.

items.name: Alpha gate
items.text: A candidate must pass all of: an economic reason to exist; net Sharpe above 0.40 and an improvement to the book; a Deflated Sharpe above 0.95 at the true number of trials; a probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) check when it was picked from a grid; a block-bootstrap 5th-percentile Sharpe above zero; a sensitivity plateau; acceptable crisis windows; and correlation to the book below 0.3.

items.name: Trial ledger
items.text: Every configuration is written to a ledger before it runs, with its decision rule fixed in advance. The trial count feeds the Deflated Sharpe, so testing more ideas raises the bar.

items.name: Paper trading
items.text: Survivors paper-trade daily on a deterministic simulated broker. Trend+Carry is book-tracked (its equity comes straight from the book's returns); the reference S&P strategies are fill-based. Since v41 every row must satisfy cash + net = equity, gross ≥ |net| and daily P&L = change in equity.

limitations.title: Limitations
items: Free daily data only; no intraday execution modelling beyond a fixed slippage.
The S&P price cache lacks many delisted names, so single-stock results carry some survivorship bias (in their favour).
The live record is short (inception 2026-06-02) and too short to confirm a Sharpe ratio.
A backtest is not a forecast of future returns.

why_failed.title: Why most strategies didn't work
why_failed.intro: Most of what we tested failed. These are the reasons, each linked to its study.

items.why: The S&P 500 is the most-arbitraged, lowest-dispersion universe there is, and short-horizon edges there are smaller than realistic costs. Early gains came from our own accounting bugs (reversed short P&L, corrupted momentum days) and disappeared once those were fixed.
Its return was market beta, not drift: alpha −3.25% a year (t = −1.21), beta 0.36.
Sharpe 0.17 after costs. The anomaly has decayed since publication and is crowded.
Uncorrelated with the book (+0.06) but net Sharpe 0.24; filtering enough to survive costs left almost nothing to trade.
Sharpe 0.15. FX factors have weakened since about 2010, and adding it diluted the book.
The signal sits near an information ceiling (AUC about 0.52–0.54), so capacity overfits. The LSTM's apparent lift came from pretraining look-ahead and vanished walk-forward.
Fed properly, the PPO agent's weights stayed within 1.7% of equal weight, so it added nothing over a simple rule.

items.idea: Levering up in calm markets (v39), extra correlation scaling (v42-A3/A4), stock-bond regime filter (v42-B1)
items.why: No improvement beyond noise, or worse tail risk (the calm-market boost cut Sharpe from 1.22 to 0.86).

Even the paper-faithful version earned about zero (−0.3% a year against a claimed 49%) and traded on only 4 of 228 rebalances: its classifier only trusted one side of a two-sided trade. With clean prices it stopped trading entirely. Its two best tickers were symbols reused by later companies.

why_failed.closing: What did work was cross-asset trend plus carry, signal-level meta-labeling, the asymmetric regime de-risk and the TREND signal. They worked because of diversification across asset classes, convexity in crises, and risk control rather than prediction.

glossary.text: The probability that a strategy's true Sharpe exceeds the best Sharpe you would expect from the same number of pure-noise trials, adjusted for sample length, skew and fat tails (Bailey and López de Prado 2014).

Probability of backtest overfitting: split the history into blocks, pick the best configuration in-sample on each combination of blocks, and count how often it ranks below median out-of-sample (Bailey et al. 2017).
Resample the daily returns in 21-day blocks (keeping short-run autocorrelation) 5,000 times and recompute the Sharpe; the 5th percentile is a pessimistic estimate.

Cross-validation that removes training samples whose label windows overlap the test fold, plus an embargo after it. CPCV repeats this over many fold combinations to get a distribution of out-of-sample scores (López de Prado 2018).
A second model that decides whether to act on (and how much to size) a signal produced by a primary rule, instead of predicting price direction itself.
A trade is labelled by which it hits first: a profit barrier, a loss barrier, or a time limit.
Every model is fitted only on data before the period it is used on, then refitted as time moves on.
The backtest trades only stocks that were index members on each date, including later-removed names, which avoids survivorship bias.
